title: ResolvedSessionConfig
description: The output of layered resolution (defaults, tenant, profile, session overrides, then language/channel/role overlays). Resolved once in the control plane, hashed, stored with the session and handed to the worker as a finished document. This is one of exactly two contact points between the Go and Python halves of the platform.

configHash.description: Hex SHA-256 over the RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) serialization of this document with configHash itself omitted. The scheme is named rather than implied: 'canonical JSON' is not one thing, and Go and Python order keys, escape unicode and render numbers differently, so an unnamed scheme yields two hashes for one document and proves nothing at the moment somebody audits a specific call.

privacyMode.description: An agent that transcribes or responds must decrypt the audio, so end-to-end encryption and AI participation are mutually exclusive unless the agent holds a key. Enforced at the control plane, not by convention.

residency.description: Providers and storage are filtered to allowed regions at resolution time; a violation is an error now, not at first use.

allowedRegions.description: Opaque provider-scoped region tokens. Deliberately not matched against one cloud's naming convention: Dafter has no home region and prescribes no cloud, and AWS, GCP, Azure and others disagree on the shape ('ap-south-1', 'asia-south1', 'centralindia'). Which tokens are permitted is a residency policy decision, not something a regex can express.

pool.description: The worker pool this session dispatches to, addressed by name over the media server's own protocol. A config field rather than a constant, so a second pool can serve one language or tenant without a rewrite.

mode.description: Cascaded is the default. Half-cascade and speech-to-speech are provider modes, and switching is a config edit.

personaRef.description: Reference to a prompt/persona document. Never inline prose.

ProviderRef.description: Providers are named by variable and pinned by model version, so a vendor silently upgrading a model cannot silently change a consumer's agent.

Addressing.description: When the agent speaks. A session without this block behaves as mode always, the agent answering every turn of the one participant it is linked to, which is what every session did before the block existed.

mode.description: always: the agent is linked to one participant and answers every turn of theirs. transcript: every human in the call is transcribed separately by the session's STT provider, the agent stays dormant and silent until one of them says its name, answers that person, and goes dormant again after the follow-up window; this sends every human's speech to the STT provider, not only the speech meant for the agent. on_device: the name is spotted locally before any audio leaves the worker; declared so a document can ask for it, and refused by the worker as an unsupported capability until a spotter is built.

name.description: What people call the agent, in the script the session's language is usually transcribed in. A mode that waits to be called needs one, which is a cross-field rule.

aliases.description: Other spellings of the same name, one per script or common transcription, for example the Devanagari, Kannada and Telugu spellings of a Latin name. Every alias counts as the name in every language, because people in one call mix languages and a recognizer does not always transcribe a name in the session language's script.

nearMisses.description: Words one letter away from the name that must never wake the agent: other people's names and ordinary words that a recognizer or a tolerant matcher would otherwise take for it. A near miss that is also the name or an alias contradicts itself, which is a cross-field rule.

followUpWindowMs.description: How long the agent stays awake for the person who called it after it has finished speaking, so a follow-up question needs no name. Counted from the end of the agent's reply, not from the wake.

Pipeline.description: Stage assembly. With a realtime provider the stt/llm/tts stages collapse and the rest is unchanged.

Turn.description: Every bad voice demo fails here, not on the LLM. Semantic turn detectors are English-trained and degrade elsewhere, which is why strategy resolves per language rather than globally.

endpointingMaxDelayMs.description: The longest the agent waits once speech has stopped: under the semantic strategy, the wait when the turn detector judges the caller unlikely to be done, and the ceiling its learned delay never passes.

localVadEnabled.description: Whether a local VAD takes part in deciding the user's turn, as it does under the vad and semantic strategies. False under provider_endpointing, where the recognizer's own VAD decides the turn and a second detector deciding it would fight the first. A local VAD that only catches the caller talking over the agent is interruption.localVadEnabled.

preemptiveGeneration.description: Start the reply on the transcript while the turn is still being decided, and keep it when the turn ends on that transcript. Where the recognizer ends the turn together with its final transcript there is nothing to overlap, so this pays off under the semantic strategy.

tts.description: Synthesize the preemptive reply too, not only generate it; spends TTS on replies a continuing turn discards.

localVadEnabled.description: Run the local VAD in agent.pipeline.vad to detect the caller starting to talk over the agent, without it deciding the end of the turn, so barge-in does not wait for the recognizer's first transcript. One VAD serves both jobs, so it is implied wherever turn.localVadEnabled is true.

Media.description: How a participant publishes, and how a recording of the room is encoded. All but egress are applied by the publishing client and the media server only routes what it is handed, which is exactly why the platform states them: an unset knob is a library default nobody chose, and a session whose profile is not in the resolved document cannot be explained after the call.

EgressProfile.description: How a server-side recording is encoded. This is the one part of the media profile the platform applies itself rather than the publishing client: encoding is a per-request field on the media server's egress API, sent by the control plane when it starts a recording. It applies to the composite layouts only. A track egress copies the published bytes and encodes nothing, so this block is not consulted for it, and a recording whose layout is 'track' plays back at whatever the publisher sent. Every field here names something the egress service is known to honor, read from its source rather than its documentation: a field it would accept and ignore is a setting the manifest would record and the recording would not have.

preset.description: One of the media server's named encoding presets, spelled in lower case. An alternative to the explicit fields, not a base for them: a document that carries both has given two answers to one question, which is a cross-field rule. Layers merge and a merge cannot delete a key, so a preset can only be set where no lower layer states an explicit field.

width.description: Pixels. Even, because the encoder subsamples chroma at 2x2 and refuses an odd dimension.

videoBitrate.description: Kilobits per second, the unit the egress API takes. Deliberately not the bits per second of the publish profile's maxBitrate: this is the recording's target rate, and the two answer different questions.

videoCodec.description: H.264 only, in its three profiles. The egress service transcodes to nothing else through this field: its enum also names VP8, which the service accepts and then ignores, and VP9 and AV1 are not in it at all. A member here that the recording could not actually be encoded with would be a guarantee nobody enforces. The publish codec is a separate choice; VP9 in the room and H.264 in the file is the normal case.

EncryptionProfile.description: How media is encrypted between participants. Derived from privacyMode at resolution so the hashed document states it rather than implying it: open is transport encryption only, sealed and trusted_agent are end to end. A layer that says otherwise contradicts the privacy mode, which is a cross-field rule.

mode.description: transport: the media server terminates encryption and sees plaintext, so agents and server-side egress work. e2ee: frames are encrypted by the publishing client and the media server forwards ciphertext, so every participant must hold a key and nothing server-side can record or transcode.

keyModel.description: Who mints and holds the end-to-end key. server_shared: one random key per session, minted by the control plane and handed to the roles the privacy mode allows, which proves encryption against the media server and the network but not against the control plane. A consumer-held key is the follow-up, and it is a second member here rather than a change of shape.

enabled.description: Off for a channel that carries no video. Stated rather than omitted because overlays compose by merging, and a merge can override a key but cannot delete one.

codec.description: VP9 and AV1 compress substantially better than VP8 and H.264 at equal quality, and both are layered rather than simulcast. The cost is encode time on the publisher's device, which is why the choice is config and not a constant.

backupCodec.description: Published alongside the primary codec for subscribers that cannot decode it. Restricted to the two codecs every endpoint can decode.

scalabilityMode.description: Spatial and temporal layer count for a layered codec, as L<spatial>T<temporal> with an optional key-frame suffix. Meaningless without VP9 or AV1, which is a cross-field rule rather than something this pattern can express.

resolution.description: Capture and publish size, named rather than given as a width and height so it stays one token that a bitrate and framerate can be matched against. 'auto' hands the choice to the publishing client, which is the only party that knows what its camera and its hardware encoder actually do well. That is different from leaving this field out: an absent field is a decision nobody made, while 'auto' is a decision to delegate, and it is recorded in the hashed document like any other. The bitrate and framerate ceilings still apply, so delegating the size never delegates the bandwidth - a client that picks a size its ceiling cannot carry gets a soft picture rather than a bigger bill.

maxBitrate.description: Bits per second, the actual uplink ceiling. Paired with a resolution: a ceiling far below what a preset needs degrades continuously instead of failing, which is worse than refusing it.

simulcast.description: Publish several bitrate versions so a subscriber pulls the size it needs. A layered codec supersedes this for its own stream, so it governs the backup codec's path.

dynacast.description: Pause layers nobody subscribes to, which saves publisher uplink rather than subscriber downlink.

adaptiveStream.description: Subscribe-side: drop quality by how large the video actually renders.

red.description: Redundant encoding: survives packet loss by roughly doubling audio bitrate.

dtx.description: Stop sending during silence. Voice is mostly silence, so this is the cheapest audio saving there is.

echoCancellation.description: Stated rather than left to the browser default, so the resolved document records what a session actually ran with.

noiseCancellation.description: Which filter the publishing client puts in front of its microphone. off asks for no suppression at all; native is the browser's own suppression, applied as a capture constraint; rnnoise is the RNNoise WASM filter attached to the track as a processor, with the browser's own suppression turned off, because two suppressors in series fight each other. Echo cancellation is separate and stays on in every mode. Every member has something implementing it: a member with no mechanism behind it is a guarantee nobody enforces.

layout.description: A track egress attaches to a published track and cannot start before the participant publishes, so no-gap coverage requires room_composite started at session creation.

consentArtifactId.description: Recording and storage cannot proceed without a valid artifact. Consent is a gate in the control plane, not a flag a consumer can forget to check.

Budgets.description: Budgets live in config so violations alert automatically instead of regressing silently.

bargeInStopP50Ms.description: Median time from the caller starting to talk over the agent to the agent leaving the speaking state.
